strengths: The paper addresses a practically important NLP question: how annotation requirements change when choosing between small task-specialized models and general language models. Comparing learning curves across eight datasets and four adaptation strategies is useful beyond comparisons at a single training-set size.

The substantial repetition—100 runs for fine-tuning, 20 for most other settings, and 10 for the API model—is a meaningful strength. It demonstrates that comparisons based on single runs can be unreliable.

The dataset-level curves and Table 1 expose substantial heterogeneity, including settings where a variance-adjusted crossing is never reached. These detailed observations could support a valuable empirical contribution.
The linked source repository, documented prompts, training details, and additional model and quantization comparisons support reproducibility and further investigation.
weaknesses: The headline annotation recommendation is insufficiently supported. Section 4 recommends approximately 100 annotations for fine-tuning, but averaging the eight mean-performance crossings in Table 1 gives 680 labels against prompting and approximately 1,941 against in-context learning. Individual crossings reach 9,000 labels against in-context learning. A crossing of aggregated performance curves is different from an average task-specific label requirement; the aggregation and its practical interpretation need to be explicit.

The second break-even criterion does not establish the claimed reliability. Comparing one model's mean minus one standard deviation with another's mean plus one standard deviation defines a descriptive separation threshold, not worst-case performance or a calibrated probability of outperforming the alternative. The reported 100–200% increases depend on this arbitrary threshold. An explicit reliability target, run-level comparisons, and uncertainty estimates for the crossings are needed to substantiate the probabilistic interpretation.

The annotation budget and selection protocol are unclear. The manuscript describes a 60/20/20 split and early stopping without establishing whether validation labels are reduced alongside training labels or counted in the budget. It also reports the best model, precision variant, and previously evaluated shot count without specifying whether these choices use validation or test performance. These details directly affect the validity of the data-efficiency comparison.

The general-model baselines need stronger prompt validation. A single prompt engineered on Mistral is reused across models despite the acknowledged importance of prompt sensitivity. More concretely, Table 2 describes BoolQ as determining whether a passage contains an answer; BoolQ requires answering the question with yes or no. As documented, this instruction changes the task and could distort the baseline and resulting break-even counts. Correct task instructions and a modest prompt-robustness check are necessary.

The blanket claim that quantization has negligible impact is contradicted by material exceptions in the reported results. Figure 7 shows Zephyr on BoolQ at roughly 42 macro-F1 when quantized versus 68 at full precision, with substantial variance differences also visible in some settings. Appendix C acknowledges exceptions, but the abstract and recommendations remain too broad. Selecting the better precision separately for each dataset also obscures the consequences of choosing quantization prospectively.

Important experimental details remain unresolved despite the repository link. Appendix D says larger-model prompting and in-context learning were evaluated only at a 1,000-training-sample setting, whereas Section 3 describes comparisons using matched subsets as the available label count changes. This needs reconciliation, particularly for low-budget comparisons. The manuscript should also specify the crossing interpolation procedure, LoRA and quantization configurations, and generated-output-to-label mapping.

The broader recommendations exceed the controlled evidence. Class count varies together with task type and possible prior benchmark exposure, so their individual effects are not established. Table 3 provides one approximate compute value per approach without sufficient information about training budgets, sequence lengths, or inference volumes to substantiate the claimed optimal resource tradeoffs. The existing experiments are promising, but the central budget and reliability claims require clarification, reanalysis, and targeted validation before a sound Findings recommendation.
